original: 1848: Born June 7 in Paris
final_text: Born 7 June 1848 in Paris, the year of the revolutions; his maternal grandmother was the socialist writer Flora Tristan.
source_note: Birth date and Flora Tristan lineage

original: 1849-1855: Childhood in Peru (mother's family)
final_text: His father Clovis died of a heart attack on the voyage to Peru; the 18-month-old Paul grew up in Lima among his mother's Tristan Moscoso kin until 1854, then Orléans.
source_note: Father died en route; return to France 1854

original: 1865-1871: Merchant marine, then French Navy
final_text: December 1865: signed on at Le Havre as a pilot's apprentice on the clipper Luzitano, later second lieutenant on the three-master Chili; 1868 navy service on the corvette Jérôme-Napoléon.
source_note: Ship names and dates of sea service

original: 1871-1883: Successful stockbroker in Paris, Sunday painter
final_text: From 1871 a Paris Bourse stockbroker (job found via Gustave Arosa); by 1879 earning 30,000 francs a year, painting Sundays in Pissarro's garden.

original: 1883: Age 35 - Quit job to paint full-time
final_text: After the 1882 Bourse crash, in October 1883 (aged 35) he wrote to Pissarro that he would live from painting at all costs; in January 1884 the family moved to cheaper Rouen.

original: 1886: First trip to Brittany (Pont-Aven)
final_text: Summer 1886: first stay at Pont-Aven, chosen because it was cheap; an accomplished boxer and fencer, he quickly dominated the young art students there.

original: 1887: Panama and Martinique trip
final_text: 1887: with Charles Laval, dreamed of Taboga island; broke in Colón, he dug on the Panama Canal 5:30am to 6pm, was fined 4 francs for urinating in public, then Martinique June-November.
source_note: Panama canal labour, arrest, Martinique dates

original: 1888: Arles with Van Gogh (October-December) - the ear incident
final_text: 1888: Arles with Van Gogh in the Yellow House, from his arrival on 23 October until Van Gogh cut his ear on 23 December, after which Gauguin fled.

original: 1889: Brittany again, painted "The Yellow Christ"
final_text: 1889: summer and autumn again in Brittany, painting The Yellow Christ and The Green Christ; at Le Pouldu the Dutch painter Meijer de Haan discreetly supported him.
source_note: 1889 Brittany works; Meijer de Haan help

original: 1891-1893: FIRST TAHITI TRIP - painted "Spirit of the Dead Watching" (1892)
final_text: First Tahiti trip: sailed 1 April 1891, back in France August 1893; painted Spirit of the Dead Watching (Manao tupapau, 1892) on burlap.
source_note: Sailing date, return, Manao tupapau date

original: 1893-1895: Back in PARIS - broke, disillusioned, tried to sell Tahiti works
final_text: 1893-95 Paris: Degas organised and bought from his November 1893 Durand-Ruel show while Monet, Renoir and Pissarro mocked it; his February 1895 Hôtel Drouot auction failed.

original: 1895-1901: SECOND TAHITI TRIP - painted masterpieces including "Where Do We Come From?" (1897), "Nevermore" (1897)
final_text: Second Tahiti stay: sailed 28 June 1895, arrived September 1895, left for the Marquesas 1901; painted Nevermore (1897) and Where Do We Come From? (1897-98).
source_note: 1895 departure; Where Do We Come From dated 1897-98

original: 1901: Moved to Marquesas Islands (Hiva Oa, Atuona)
final_text: Arrived at Atuona, Hiva Oa, on 16 September 1901, and bought land in the town centre from the Catholic mission after first attending mass regularly.
source_note: Arrival date and land bought from mission

original: 1901-1903: ATUONA PERIOD - "Riders on the Beach" (1902), final works
final_text: Atuona 1901-03: painted landscapes and figure studies with Vollard's clients in mind, plus Riders on the Beach (1902, Museum Folkwang, Essen).
source_note: Marquesas output aimed at Vollard clientele

original: 1903: Died May 8, age 54, in Atuona
final_text: Died suddenly on the morning of 8 May 1903 in Atuona, aged 54; his neighbour Tioka found him at 11 o'clock.
source_note: Death date, age, found by Tioka

original: "Vision After the Sermon" (1888) - Jacob wrestling angel, Breton women
final_text: Vision After the Sermon (1888): Breton women see Jacob wrestle the angel; painted for the church at Nizon, refused by its priest; Edinburgh bought it in 1925 for £1,150.

original: "The Yellow Christ" (1889) - crucifixion with Breton landscape
final_text: The Yellow Christ (1889): its Christ copies a 17th-century painted wooden crucifix in the Trémalo chapel near Pont-Aven; now Buffalo AKG Art Museum.

original: "Ia Orana Maria" (1891) - Tahitian Madonna
final_text: Ia Orana Maria (1891, Met): a Tahitian Madonna and child pointed out by a yellow-winged angel; the composition is based on his photograph of a Borobudur relief.

original: "Spirit of the Dead Watching/Manao tupapau" (1892) - girl on bed, spirit behind
final_text: Manao tupapau (1892), on burlap: Teha'amana lies face down, a spirit-woman behind; he wrote Mette on 8 Dec 1892 that the pose was 'on the verge of being indecent'.
source_note: Burlap support; letter to Mette 8 Dec 1892

original: "Arearea" (1892) - two women, red dog
final_text: Arearea (1892, Musée d'Orsay): two women and a red dog that drew sarcasm at the 1893 Durand-Ruel show; Gauguin bought it back in 1895 before leaving Europe.

original: "Woman with Mango/Vahine no te vi" (1892) - NOT 1896
final_text: Vahine no te vi (Woman of the Mango), 1892 not 1896, Baltimore Museum of Art; Edgar Degas bought it in 1895.

original: "Mahana no atua/Day of the God" (1894) - memory of Tahiti
final_text: Mahana no atua (1894, Art Institute of Chicago) was painted in Paris from memory; its idol of the goddess Hina derives from photographs of Borobudur reliefs.
source_note: Painted in Paris; Hina from Borobudur

original: Worked on woodcuts, ceramics
final_text: In Paris he cut the Noa Noa woodcuts (1894) with an experimental technique and fired the stoneware Oviri that winter, showing it at the 1895 Société Nationale salon.
source_note: Noa Noa woodcuts; Oviri at 1895 salon

original: "Te Tamari No Atua/Nativity" (1896) - Tahitian nativity
final_text: Te tamari no atua (1896, Neue Pinakothek, Munich): a Polynesian Nativity painted as Pahura gave birth around Christmas 1896; the baby girl died in infancy.

original: "Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?" (1897) - 4m masterpiece, painted before suicide attempt
final_text: Where Do We Come From? (1897-98, MFA Boston) is 139 x 375 cm, about 3.75 m; after finishing it he tried to kill himself with arsenic, months after daughter Aline died.
source_note: Dimensions; arsenic suicide attempt after completion

original: "Nevermore" (1897) - reclining nude, raven
final_text: Nevermore (1897, Courtauld): Pahura nude on a bed; Gauguin called the bird a devil's bird, not Poe's raven; Delius bought it in 1898 for 500 francs via Monfreid.

original: "Two Tahitian Women" (1899) - breasts, mangos
final_text: Two Tahitian Women (1899, Met): one woman holds mango blossoms, not mangoes; the same pair reappears in Faa Iheihe (Tate) and Rupe Rupe (Pushkin Museum).

original: "Contes Barbares/Primitive Tales" (1902)
final_text: Contes barbares (1902, Museum Folkwang): the crouching claw-footed figure behind two Polynesian women is Meijer de Haan, his Brittany friend, dead since 1895.

original: "Riders on the Beach" (1902) - pink sand
final_text: Riders on the Beach (1902, Museum Folkwang, Essen): horsemen on a pink beach, a colour often read as anticipating Fauvism; a second version also exists.

original: "Self-Portrait Near Golgotha" (1903) - one of last works
final_text: Self-Portrait near Golgotha dates from 1896, not 1903 (MASP, São Paulo); it was found among his belongings after his death.

original: "I am a savage" - rejected European civilization
final_text: In a 1903 letter to Charles Morice: 'You were wrong that day when you said I was wrong to say I was a savage. It's true enough: I am a savage.'

original: "Art is either plagiarism or revolution"
final_text: 'Art is either plagiarism or revolution' is traced to a letter in Le Soir, 25 April 1895; the popular wording spread via James Huneker's paraphrase (1913).

original: "Life has no meaning unless one lives it with a will"
final_text: Dec 1902-Feb 1903, sick in Atuona, he wrote the memoir Avant et après, ending with a philosophy of life as a struggle to reconcile opposites.
source_note: Avant et après written in Atuona

original: "Don't copy nature too literally. Art is abstraction."
final_text: To Schuffenecker, Pont-Aven, 14 August 1888: 'Don't copy nature too much. Art is an abstraction; derive this abstraction from nature while dreaming before it.'

original: Color has its own emotional language
final_text: In Martinique (1887) he began setting analogous colours side by side for a muted effect, soon moving to non-representational colour with a life of its own.

original: Sought the "primitive" as authentic truth
final_text: His 'primitive' Tahiti was partly bookish: he was lent Moerenhout's 1837 Voyage aux îles du Grand Océan to learn the island's forgotten religion.
source_note: Moerenhout book source of Tahitian myths

original: Synthetism: flat areas of bold color, dark outlines
final_text: Synthetism's debut: the June 1889 Volpini show at the Café des Arts, filling walls left bare when the owner's Italian mirrors arrived late; Gauguin hung 11 zincographs on yellow paper.

original: Cloisonnism: inspired by stained glass, Japanese prints, medieval enamels
final_text: 'Cloisonnism' was coined by critic Édouard Dujardin in the Revue indépendante, March 1888, for Louis Anquetin's paintings; Bernard and Gauguin then worked in the style.

original: Mixed memory, imagination, observation - never purely from life
final_text: He took to Tahiti photographs and prints, including a Borobudur temple frieze and an Egyptian fresco, which he called 'a whole little world of friends' in a letter to Redon.
source_note: Photographs carried to Tahiti; Redon letter

original: Used local Polynesian pigments - earth colors, crushed flowers
final_text: No source for Polynesian flower pigments; documented instead: he painted on coarse burlap, as in Manao tupapau (1892).

original: Carved wood frames as part of the artwork
final_text: He carved wood from his stockbroker years: a carved and painted mahogany medallion of the singer Valérie Roumi (1880), now in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek.

original: Legend says he painted "Paradise on Earth" days before death
final_text: Legend says he painted "Paradise on Earth" days before death
source_note: the novel's own lore (Ule's lost Gauguin) — fiction by design, kept
rejected_replacement: No 'Paradise on Earth' is recorded. Real story: at the 1903 Papeete sale Breton Village in the Snow was shown upside down as 'Niagara Falls'; Victor Segalen bought it.

original: Never catalogued, possibly destroyed or hidden
final_text: Never catalogued, possibly destroyed or hidden
source_note: the novel's own lore (Ule's lost Gauguin) — fiction by design, kept
rejected_replacement: Without a will, his lesser effects were sold in Atuona and his letters, manuscripts and paintings auctioned in Papeete on 5 September 1903; Segalen bought seven paintings.

original: Some say buried with him, others that locals preserved it
final_text: Some say buried with him, others that locals preserved it
source_note: the novel's own lore (Ule's lost Gauguin) — fiction by design, kept
rejected_replacement: Breton Village in the Snow, long believed his last painting, stayed with Segalen's family until 1952, when France's national museums acquired it.

original: The ultimate Gauguin mystery
final_text: The ultimate Gauguin mystery
source_note: the novel's own lore (Ule's lost Gauguin) — fiction by design, kept
rejected_replacement: A real mystery: four teeth in a bottle at the bottom of his Atuona well, DNA-linked to Gauguin, held no mercury, so he either lacked syphilis or was never treated.

original: "Maison du Jouir" (House of Pleasure) with provocative carvings
final_text: Maison du Jouir: two-storey house built with tattooed carpenter Tioka; carved lintels read 'Soyez amoureuses vous serez heureuses', 'Soyez mystérieuses'; four of five pieces at Orsay.

original: Living in poverty, legs covered in eczema/syphilis sores
final_text: Sores on his legs were treated with arsenic; he called them eczema; syphilis is unproven. His ankle, shattered in an 1894 Concarneau brawl, never healed.
source_note: Eczema claim; no direct syphilis evidence

original: Addicted to morphine and absinthe for pain
final_text: By September 1902 he took morphine injections, then handed his syringe set to a neighbour and used laudanum; an empty laudanum bottle stood by his deathbed.

original: Fighting Bishop Martin and colonial authorities
final_text: He fought Bishop Martin over mission schools and carved Père Paillard (Father Lechery, 1902, NGA Washington), a horned bishop displayed outside his house.
source_note: NGA: Père Paillard lampoons Bishop Martin

original: Sentenced to prison for defamation (died before serving)
final_text: On 27 March 1903 a local magistrate fined him 500 francs and gave him three months for libelling a gendarme; he appealed to Papeete and died before the hearing.
source_note: Sentence date and terms; appeal pending

original: Still painting, demanding art supplies by mail
final_text: Vollard's deal (from 1900): 300 francs a month against at least 25 paintings a year at 200 francs, plus art materials; Gauguin sent him twenty canvases in April 1902.

original: Last words reportedly: "I have been defeated"
final_text: No deathbed words are recorded; in his last letter to Charles Morice, weeks before death, he wrote: 'I am on the ground, but not yet defeated.'

original: Buried in Calvary Cemetery, Atuona - grave overlooks bay
final_text: Buried in Atuona's Catholic Calvary Cemetery at 2pm the day after his death; a bronze cast of his Oviri was set on the grave in 1973, as he had wished.
